chapter_title: Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent
learning_objective: The learner will calculate whether two IPv4 addresses are on the same network, given a netmask, in 8 cases, with at least 7 of 8 correct.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** same-subnet-checker
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Apply
**Bloom Verb:** calculate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate whether two IPv4 addresses are on the same network, given a netmask, in 8 cases, with at least 7 of 8 correct. **Prerequisites:** IP address, netmask, network address, same network, binary form of a number from 0 to 255 (all defined in this chapter above this block; binary numbers are in Chapter 3). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the 8 cases the learner chooses "same network" or "different networks", then types the network address of the first device. A case is correct when both answers match the Answer columns in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Using the explorer (typing any addresses and watching the binary AND) is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Addresses that start with the same number are always on the same network. (2) A mask can only fall between whole numbers. (3) The all-zeros and all-ones device addresses can be given to a device. **Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation requires the learner to carry out the mask-and-compare procedure on new numbers. Showing the two addresses and the mask in binary, with the mask's 1 bits highlighted, ties the procedure to what the mask keeps, and asking for the network address as well as the yes/no answer shows the work. **Content:** The explorer shows an address, a second address, and a netmask. Each is shown as four numbers and as four groups of 8 bits. The sim computes the network address of each as the bitwise AND of the address and the mask. The two addresses are on the same network when the two network addresses are equal. | # | First address | Netmask | Second address | Same network? | Network address of the first | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 192.168.1.23 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.1.50 | same | 192.168.1.0 | The mask keeps the first three numbers, and both start 192.168.1. | | 2 | 192.168.1.23 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.2.50 | different | 192.168.1.0 | The third numbers, 1 and 2, differ and the mask keeps them. | | 3 | 10.4.7.88 | 255.255.0.0 | 10.4.200.9 | same | 10.4.0.0 | The mask keeps only 10.4, and both start 10.4. | | 4 | 10.4.7.88 | 255.255.255.0 | 10.4.200.9 | different | 10.4.7.0 | The same two addresses, but this mask also keeps the third number, 7 and 200. | | 5 | 172.16.5.5 | 255.255.240.0 | 172.16.15.1 | same | 172.16.0.0 | 240 is 11110000, so only the top 4 bits of the third number are kept; 5 and 15 are both 0000. | | 6 | 172.16.5.5 | 255.255.240.0 | 172.16.16.1 | different | 172.16.0.0 | 16 is 00010000, so its kept bits are 0001, not 0000. | | 7 | 192.168.1.200 | 255.255.255.128 | 192.168.1.20 | different | 192.168.1.128 | 128 is 10000000: 200 keeps the top bit (1) and 20 keeps 0. | | 8 | 192.168.1.130 | 255.255.255.128 | 192.168.1.200 | same | 192.168.1.128 | 130 and 200 are both 128 or more, so both keep the top bit 1. | For exploration the learner can type any two addresses (each number 0 to 255) and choose a netmask from 255.255.255.0, 255.255.255.128, 255.255.240.0 or 255.255.0.0. The default is 192.168.1.23, 255.255.255.0 and 192.168.1.50. **Provenance:** The arithmetic is the chapter sections "The Netmask" and "The Local Network", and the same cases (1 to 6) are in the table printed by `02-ip-and-subnet.py`. The addresses are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative." **Rules:** The network address is the bitwise AND of each of the four numbers of the address with the matching number of the mask. Two addresses are on the same network when their network addresses are equal. If the learner types a number outside 0 to 255, the sim ignores the change and keeps the previous value. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner opens the explorer and changes the second address's last number, watching its bits and the kept bits change. 2. The learner changes the netmask from 255.255.255.0 to 255.255.0.0 and notices which cases flip from different to same. 3. The learner starts the 8 cases. Case 1 is shown. 4. The learner chooses same or different, types the first address's network address, and submits. 5. The sim highlights the kept bits of both addresses and shows the Why text. 6. After case 8, the sim shows the score. The learner should notice that cases 3 and 4 use the same two addresses and have opposite answers. **Feedback:** 8 cases, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. They are , and the network address is : ". The answer is revealed right after each submission, and a running score "n of 8" is shown. **Starting State:** The explorer shows 192.168.1.23 and 192.168.1.50 with 255.255.255.0, with the question "Are these two on the same network?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the netmask keeps the network part of an address, that 255.255.240.0 keeps the top 4 bits of the third number, that 172.16.5.5 and 172.16.15.1 are on the same network under that mask while 172.16.16.1 is not, and that a network with \( h \) host bits has \( 2^h - 2 \) usable addresses.
